nodes.note: The geometric proofs use reflections to find a minimal path representing the perimeter. The orthic triangle also gives a periodic light path in a mirrored acute triangle.

nodes.name: Parallelogram law
nodes.statement: In Euclidean geometry, in a parallelogram ABCD the sum of the squares of the lengths of the four sides equals the sum of the squares of the lengths of the two diagonals: 2AB² + 2BC² = AC² + BD².
nodes.note: For a rectangle it reduces to the Pythagorean theorem. In an inner product space the same identity 2‖x‖² + 2‖y‖² = ‖x+y‖² + ‖x−y‖² holds, and a norm that satisfies it must come from an inner product.

nodes.name: Angle bisector theorem
nodes.statement: In a triangle ABC, if the bisector of angle A meets side BC at a point D between B and C, then |BD| / |CD| = |AB| / |AC|. Conversely, if a point D on side BC divides BC in the ratio |AB| : |AC|, then AD bisects angle A.
nodes.by: Appears in Euclid's Elements, Book VI, Proposition 3
nodes.note: An immediate consequence is that the bisector of the vertex angle of an isosceles triangle also bisects the opposite side.

nodes.name: Tarski's circle-squaring problem
nodes.statement: A disc in the plane can be cut into finitely many pieces that can be moved by translations alone and reassembled into a square of equal area.
nodes.by: Posed by Alfred Tarski, 1925; proved by Miklós Laczkovich, 1990
nodes.note: Laczkovich's pieces are non-measurable, and his proof uses the axiom of choice. Andrew Marks and Spencer Unger gave a constructive solution with Borel pieces in 2017, and pieces with Jordan curve boundaries cannot work.

nodes.name: Simson line theorem
nodes.statement: Given a triangle ABC and a point P on its circumcircle, the three points on lines AB, AC and BC that are closest to P lie on one line. Conversely, if the three closest points to P on three lines, no two of them parallel, lie on one line, then P lies on the circumcircle of the triangle formed by the three lines.
nodes.by: Named for Robert Simson; first published by William Wallace, 1799
nodes.note: Because Wallace published it first, the line is sometimes called the Wallace line.

nodes.name: Bottema's theorem
nodes.statement: In a triangle ABC, build squares on the two sides AC and BC, both on the same side as one follows the triangle's vertices around (both to the left or both to the right). Then, keeping A and B fixed, the midpoint of the segment joining the two square vertices opposite C does not depend on the position of C.
nodes.by: Linked to Oene Bottema, who published a simple proof; the theorem was known before
nodes.note: If S is the projection of that midpoint M onto AB, then AS = BS = MS.

nodes.name: Conway circle theorem
nodes.statement: At each vertex of a triangle, extend the two sides meeting there beyond that vertex by the length of the opposite side. The six endpoints of the three resulting line segments lie on a circle whose centre is the incentre of the triangle.
nodes.by: Named after John Horton Conway
nodes.note: The radius of this circle is √(r² + s²), where r is the inradius and s the semiperimeter of the triangle.

nodes.name: Kepler conjecture
nodes.statement: No arrangement of equally sized spheres filling three-dimensional Euclidean space has a greater average density than the cubic close packing (face-centered cubic) and hexagonal close packing arrangements. Their density is π/(3√2), about 74.05%.
nodes.by: Stated by Johannes Kepler, 1611; proof announced by Thomas Hales, 1998
nodes.note: Gauss proved in 1831 that it holds when the spheres are arranged in a regular lattice. Hales' proof is a proof by exhaustion using computer calculations, and a formal proof was accepted by Forum of Mathematics, Pi in 2017.

nodes.name: Erdős–Mordell inequality
nodes.statement: For any triangle ABC and any point P inside it, let PL, PM and PN be the perpendiculars from P to the lines containing the three sides. Then PA + PB + PC ≥ 2(PL + PM + PN), so the sum of the distances from P to the sides is at most half the sum of the distances from P to the vertices.
nodes.by: Named after Paul Erdős and Louis Mordell; Erdős posed the problem in 1935 and Barrow proved it in 1937
nodes.note: Equality holds only for the equilateral triangle with P at its centroid. Barrow's inequality is a stronger version in which the distances to the sides are replaced by the distances to the points where the angle bisectors at P cross the sides.
